question.explanation:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem \[ \Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0) = I_n, \] where $I_n$ is the identity matrix.

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

\begin{align*} e^{At} &= \alpha_1 A t + \alpha_0 I \\[5pt] &= \alpha_1 \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} t + \alpha_0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_0 & 2 \alpha_1 t \\ 2 \alpha_1 t & \alpha_0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are \[ \lambda_1=-2t, \qquad \lambda_2=2t, \] both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

\begin{align*} \begin{cases} r(-2t) = e^{-2t} \\[3pt] r(2t) = e^{2t} \end{cases} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} -2t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{-2t} \\[3pt] 2t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{2t} \end{cases} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

  • Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get \[ -4t\alpha_1 = e^{-2t} - e^{2t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_1 = -\dfrac{1}{4t}(e^{-2t}-e^{2t}). \]

  • Adding the first and the second equations, we get \[ 2\alpha_0 = e^{-2t} + e^{2t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{-2t}+e^{2t}). \]

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} \alpha_0 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{-2t}+e^{2t}) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{2t}+e^{-2t}) \\[10pt] 2 \alpha_1 t &= 2 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{4t}(e^{-4t}-e^{4t}) \right) t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{2t}-e^{-2t}) \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} {e^{2t}+e^{-2t}} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{e^{2t}-e^{-2t}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{e^{2t}-e^{-2t}} & e^{2t}+e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: \[ \mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_1(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t}, \quad \mathbf{x}_2(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t} \] Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2,$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
question.explanation:
Given a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A \mathbf{x},$ where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, a fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ of the system is an $n \times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2 \times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1(t) &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{x}_2(t) &= \begin{bmatrix} t \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t} = \begin{bmatrix} t e^{2t} \\ e^{2t} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as \[ \Phi(t) = \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} & t e^{2t} \\ 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Note: The columns of $\Phi$ can be written in any order.

question.explanation:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem \[ \Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0) = I_n, \] where $I_n$ is the identity matrix.

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, \begin{align*} e^{At} &= \alpha_1 A t + \alpha_0 I \\[5pt] &= \alpha_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} t + \alpha_0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \alpha_1 t + \alpha_0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \alpha_1 t + \alpha_0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are \[ \lambda_1 = 2t \quad\text{and}\quad \lambda_2 = 5t \] each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following: \begin{align*} \begin{cases} r(2t) = e^{2t} \\[3pt] r(5t) = e^{5t} \end{cases} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 2t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{2t} \\[3pt] 5t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{5t} \end{cases} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

  • Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get \[ \alpha_1 = \frac{e^{5t} - e^{2t}}{3t}. \]

  • Substituting this into the first equation, we get \[ 2t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{2t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_0 = \frac{5e^{2t} - 2e^{5t}}{3}. \]

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following: \begin{align*} 2 \alpha_1 t + \alpha_0 &= 2t \cdot \frac{e^{5t} - e^{2t}}{3t} + \frac{5e^{2t} - 2e^{5t}}{3} \\[5pt] &= e^{2t} \\[10pt] 5 \alpha_1 t + \alpha_0 &= 5t \cdot \frac{e^{5t} - e^{2t}}{3t} + \frac{5e^{2t} - 2e^{5t}}{3} \\[5pt] &= e^{5t} \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \Phi_0(t) =e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{e^{2t}} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{e^{5t}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

\begin{align*} \begin{cases} r(5t) = e^{5t} \\[3pt] \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda} r(5t) = e^{5t} \end{cases} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 5t\alpha_1 + \alpha_0 = e^{5t} \\[3pt] \alpha_1 = e^{5t} \end{cases} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

  • From the second equation, we get \[ \alpha_1 = e^{5t}. \]

  • Substituting this into the first one, we get \[ 5te^{5t} + \alpha_0 = e^{5t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_0 = e^{5t}(1-5t). \]

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:
